title: Waves that cancel out
subtitle: Twice random makes… certain? Interference is the trick behind every quantum algorithm.

steps.title: Odds that cancel out
body: In everyday life, probabilities only add up: if there are two paths to a result, the total chance is higher.
In the quantum world, what adds up are the amplitudes — and they have a sign (actually, a phase). One path with +½ and another with −½ cancel each other, like a wave crest meeting a trough.

steps.question: One H leaves the qubit half and half. What if we apply two H gates in a row? What's the chance of measuring 1?
steps.explain: Zero! The second H doesn't “shuffle again”: it undoes the first. The two paths leading to 1 have amplitudes +½ and −½ and cancel out. The ones leading to 0 add up to ½ + ½ = 1.

steps.title: The math behind it
body: Applying it twice starting from |0⟩, there are two paths to 1: via 0 (amplitude +½) and via 1 (amplitude −½). Sum: zero. That's destructive interference.
Quantum algorithms are choreographies of interference: making wrong answers cancel out and right ones reinforce each other.

steps.question: What if we put a Z between the two H gates? Z doesn't change any probability… What's the chance of measuring 1?
steps.explain: 100%! Z flipped the sign of one of the paths. Now it's 0 that cancels and 1 that reinforces. An “invisible” phase decided the result.

steps.title: 1 without X
steps.goal: Take the qubit to |1⟩ with certainty — but the X gate isn't available.
hints: You just saw this trick in the previous step.
steps.success: H·Z·H = X. You built a NOT using nothing but interference.

steps.title: Phases add up
steps.goal: Between the two fixed H gates, rotate the phase enough for the qubit to read 1 with certainty. Only S and T available.
hints: You need half a turn (180°) of phase, like Z.
steps.success: Two S's = one Z. Four T's would work too. On the sphere, each gate turned the arrow along the equator; at the end, H turned the phase into a result.

steps.title: Interference in your ears
steps.text: Noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference of sound: a microphone picks up the noise and the headphone plays the same wave with its sign flipped. Crest meets trough, and the noise disappears. Quantum amplitudes work in a similar way — just with possibilities instead of air pressure.

steps.question: Two Z gates in a row are equivalent to what?

options.why: Z doesn't swap 0 and 1: it only touches phase. Two half turns around the vertical axis don't take the arrow to the other pole.
Right. Two half turns = one full turn. The sign of |1⟩ flips and flips back.
H mixes poles and equator. Z never does that, not even repeated.

takeaways: Amplitudes add up with phase: they can reinforce or cancel each other.
H followed by H goes back to the start; H·Z·H becomes an X.
Phase is invisible in a direct measurement, but decides the result when there's interference.
